The table below is the one-glance summary. Each section below expands on one platform, and the later sections compare them on cost, developer availability, and fit.

Shopify is the most common choice for D2C brands, and for good reason: it is the fastest way to launch an ecommerce store, it handles most of the technical maintenance for you, and there is a deep pool of Shopify developers to hire from. The trade-off is that you are building on someone else's platform, and some customization you want will be limited by what Shopify supports.

items: A standard Shopify store can go live in a few weeks, not months.
Shopify handles hosting, security, and platform updates, which removes a large ongoing burden.
There are more Shopify developers than any other platform, especially in India and Southeast Asia.
Most standard ecommerce features (subscriptions, reviews, loyalty, email) are available as apps.
Shopify Payments simplifies PCI compliance significantly.
Some checkout, cart, and backend logic cannot be customised on Shopify, and you have to work within the platform's model.
Many features require apps, and each app adds subscription cost and potential performance impact.
If you use a third-party payment gateway instead of Shopify Payments, Shopify charges an additional transaction fee.
Migrating away from Shopify is possible but non-trivial. You are committing to the platform for the medium term.

blocks.text: When Shopify is the right fit

inline: Shopify is the right fit for D2C brands launching fast, subscription and membership stores, stores with a standard product catalog and standard checkout needs, and teams that do not want to maintain hosting and infrastructure. If your requirements are mostly standard ecommerce and you want to be live quickly, Shopify is almost always the right answer.

WooCommerce is the WordPress-based ecommerce plugin, and it is the most flexible of the three options. It is the right choice when your requirements are non-standard, when your content and commerce need to coexist on the same site, or when you want full ownership of the platform and the data. The trade-off is that you own the maintenance burden, and that burden is real.

items: Custom logic, custom post types, complex taxonomies, and integration with the broader WordPress plugin ecosystem.
If your marketing strategy is content-heavy (blog, guides, recipes, editorial), WordPress is the strongest platform for combining content and ecommerce on one site.
You own the code, the data, and the hosting. There is no platform vendor.
The core platform and plugin are free, which makes the initial build cheaper than Shopify for the same feature set.
There are many WooCommerce developers, especially in India, Eastern Europe, and Latin America.
You are responsible for hosting, security, plugin updates, and conflict resolution. This is a real ongoing cost, not a one-off.
WooCommerce is more resource-intensive than Shopify, and a poorly optimized store can be slow.
The plugin ecosystem includes many poorly maintained plugins, and it is easy to accumulate technical debt.
WooCommerce does not handle PCI compliance for you, which means you have to be more careful about how you set up payments.

blocks.text: When WooCommerce is the right fit

inline: WooCommerce is the right fit for content-heavy stores, stores with complex custom logic, stores that need deep integration with other WordPress plugins (memberships, courses, events), and businesses that want full ownership of their platform. If your requirements are standard and you want a hands-off platform, WooCommerce is usually more work than it is worth.

A custom build (or a headless build, which is a specific type of custom build) means building the storefront and the backend separately, or building the whole stack from scratch. Headless builds typically use a modern front end (Next.js, React) and an API-first backend (Shopify's Storefront API, a headless CMS, or a custom backend). Custom builds go further and replace the backend as well.

items: You can build exactly what you need, including features no hosted platform supports.
A well-built headless or custom store can be significantly faster than a standard Shopify or WooCommerce store.
Headless architectures make it easier to sell across web, mobile, marketplaces, and in-store systems from a single backend.
Custom builds integrate cleanly with complex ERP, PIM, and CRM systems.
A custom or headless build typically starts at $50,000 and can go well past $250,000 for enterprise deployments.
Custom builds take months, not weeks. A standard build is usually 4 to 9 months, sometimes longer.
You own everything — hosting, security, updates, performance. This is the highest maintenance of the three options.
The pool of headless and custom developers is much smaller than the pool of Shopify or WooCommerce developers, which makes hiring harder and more expensive.

blocks.text: When a custom build is the right fit

inline: A custom or headless build is the right fit for enterprise stores with complex requirements, for stores that need genuine multi-channel commerce, and for businesses where the storefront experience is the product and a standard platform cannot deliver it. For most small and mid-market stores, a custom build is overkill, and a Shopify or WooCommerce store will serve you better for years.

blocks.text: What the cost comparison actually shows

inline: For a standard small store, Shopify and WooCommerce are roughly comparable on total first-year cost. Shopify tends to be slightly higher on platform subscriptions and apps, WooCommerce tends to be slightly higher on hosting and maintenance. The difference becomes decisive at the mid-market and enterprise levels, where custom builds cost 3 to 10 times more than a hosted platform.

The most common mistake is choosing a custom build for a project that would be fine on Shopify or WooCommerce, and then paying two to three times the cost for features that are not actually used. Custom builds are the right choice for a small number of stores; they are the wrong choice for most.

If you already have a store and are considering a platform change, the migration itself is a project — and it is often the biggest reason buyers overpay for a build they did not need.

The most common migration. Products, customers, and orders can be moved, but custom checkout and cart logic usually cannot be preserved. Expect to rebuild features rather than port them. Migrations usually take 6 to 12 weeks, and the cost is typically $10,000 to $40,000 depending on the store's scale.

Less common, but happens when a store outgrows Shopify's customization limits. The migration is more complex than the reverse, because you are now responsible for hosting, security, and plugins. Expect 8 to 16 weeks and $15,000 to $50,000.

A headless migration is not a platform migration — it is a rebuild of the front end while keeping the existing backend (usually Shopify). Expect 3 to 6 months and $50,000 to $150,000. Worth it only if the storefront experience is a genuine competitive advantage.

sections.title: Which Platform to Choose: A Summary

inline: If you are still deciding, here is the short version:

items: You want to launch fast and minimize maintenance.
Your store has standard ecommerce features — catalog, cart, checkout, standard payments.
You want the largest developer pool to hire from.
You do not need content and commerce tightly integrated.
Your store has custom logic that Shopify cannot support.
You have content-heavy marketing (blog, guides, recipes) that should live with the store.
You want full ownership of the platform, code, and data.
You already have a WordPress site you want to add ecommerce to.

blocks.text: Choose a custom or headless build if...

items: You have complex requirements no hosted platform can support.
You need genuine multi-channel commerce.
The storefront experience is your competitive advantage, and performance is critical.
You have the budget for a $50,000+ build and the resources to maintain it.

inline: For most stores under $30,000 in build budget, the answer is Shopify or WooCommerce. For most stores above $100,000 in build budget, the answer is a custom or headless build. The interesting decisions happen in the middle, and the right answer depends on specifics.

faqs.q: Should I build a custom ecommerce store?
a: Only if your requirements genuinely cannot be met by Shopify or WooCommerce. Custom builds are 3 to 10 times more expensive, take 3 to 9 months, and require more maintenance. For most stores under $100,000 in build budget, a custom build is overkill. See the

a: Products, customers, and orders can be migrated, but custom checkout and cart logic usually cannot be preserved. Migrations typically take 6 to 12 weeks and cost $10,000 to $40,000. See the

The core platform is free, which makes the initial build cheaper. But WooCommerce's ongoing costs (hosting, plugins, maintenance) often close the gap within a year or two. On a total first-year basis, the two are usually comparable for a standard store. See the

faqs.q: What is headless commerce, and do I need it?
a: Headless commerce means separating the storefront (front end) from the backend ecommerce platform. It offers more flexibility and performance, but costs 2 to 5 times more than a standard Shopify store and requires a much smaller pool of developers. You need it only if your requirements genuinely cannot be met by a standard platform. See the

faqs.q: Which platform is best for SEO?
a: All three can rank well if implemented correctly. Shopify's SEO is good out of the box. WooCommerce requires more SEO attention but gives you more control. Custom builds are as good as the developer builds them. Platform choice matters less than implementation and content strategy.

faqs.q: Which platform has the most developers available?
a: Shopify, by a wide margin. WooCommerce is second. Headless and custom developers are much harder to find. For city-specific availability, see

faqs.q: Can I run a store on WooCommerce without hiring a developer?
a: You can launch a very small store with a WordPress theme and WooCommerce plugin without hiring a developer, but maintaining it yourself becomes a real burden as the store grows. For anything beyond a small store, a developer is worth the cost. See
